literal: His great-great-grandfather Sou was Governor of Qi commandery under Jin.
idiomatic: Great-great-grandfather Sou was Jin's Governor of Qi commandery.

literal: Because of Jin's turmoil Sou dwelt at Anle in Qingzhou.
idiomatic: When Jin fell into chaos Sou settled at Anle in Qingzhou.

literal: Only when Shuang came did he return to his native place.
idiomatic: Shuang was the first to return home.

literal: Shuang in youth loved learning and also dipped into literature and history; he was elegantly known and prized by Prince of Zhongshan Ying.
idiomatic: Young Shuang loved books and history; Prince Ying of Zhongshan prized him.

literal: He held the post of Governor of Xihe.
idiomatic: He became Governor of Xihe.

literal: His government was clear and simple; officials and people were at ease and pleased.
idiomatic: He ruled plainly; officials and people were content.

literal: When Prince of Zhongshan Xi raised troops to execute Yuan Cha and failed, Xi's younger brother Lüe threw himself on Shuang's mercy.
idiomatic: When Prince Xi of Zhongshan rose against Yuan Cha and failed, his brother Lüe sought refuge with Shuang.

literal: Shuang hid and protected him a full year.
idiomatic: Shuang hid him for a full year.

literal: At the time the price on Lüe's head was very keen; Lüe in fear asked to be sent beyond the border.
idiomatic: Bounty hunters pressed hard; Lüe begged to be sent abroad.

literal: Shuang said: "There will be one death — that alone is hard to bear.
idiomatic: Shuang said, "Death comes once — that is the hard part.

literal: Now meeting a true friend, I view death as returning home — please do not worry on my account.
idiomatic: Now I meet a true friend and welcome death as homecoming — do not fret for me."

literal: Lüe again pressed hard to turn south; Shuang then sent his nephew Chang to escort him to the lands east of the Yangtze.
idiomatic: Lüe still begged to go south; Shuang sent nephew Chang to deliver him to the south.

literal: When Empress Dowager Ling restored the government, learning Lüe had been saved through Shuang, she summoned and appointed him Grand Master for Splendid Happiness.
idiomatic: When Empress Dowager Ling regained power she learned Lüe owed his escape to Shuang and made Lüe Grand Master for Splendid Happiness.

literal: At the time Lüe's elder sister was Princess Rao'an, wife of Diao Xuan; she repeatedly appealed to Empress Dowager Ling, begging to summon Lüe back.
idiomatic: Lüe's sister, Princess Rao'an, wife of Diao Xuan, repeatedly begged the empress dowager to recall him.

literal: The court then exchanged him for the two captives taken at Xuzhou, Jiang Ge and Zu Yunheng.
idiomatic: The court traded him for two captives from Xuzhou — Jiang Ge and Zu Yunheng.

literal: Because Shuang and Lüe were old friends, he was ordered to the border to receive him.
idiomatic: As Shuang and Lüe were old friends, Shuang was sent to the frontier to welcome him.

literal: At the end of Emperor Ming's reign he was made Governor of Western Yanzhou.
idiomatic: Late in Emperor Ming's reign he became Governor of Western Yanzhou.

literal: At the time bandits swarmed; men of the province Zhang Taogong and others gathered fugitives and openly plundered.
idiomatic: Bandits swarmed; Zhang Taogong and others rallied outlaws and robbed openly.

literal: Shuang on reaching the border first sent envoys to instruct Taogong, setting forth fortune and ruin; Taogong at once followed the envoy to confess guilt, and Shuang released him without inquiry.
idiomatic: At the border Shuang sent envoys to Taogong with warning of consequences; Taogong surrendered at once and Shuang pardoned him.

literal: Later wherever robbers struck he had Taogong pursue them; all were captured — and the province grew orderly.
idiomatic: Later he set Taogong to hunt every robbery; all were caught and the province grew quiet.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Xiaozhuang's reign he acted as Governor of Jizhou and by merit was enfeoffed Baron of Qucheng township.
idiomatic: At Xiaozhuang's start he acted as Governor of Jizhou and was made Baron of Qucheng.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Xiaowu's reign he was transferred General of Valiant Cavalry and Grand Master with the Splendor of the Left.
idiomatic: At Xiaowu's start he became General of Valiant Cavalry and Grand Master with the Splendor of the Left.

literal: In the third year of Xinghe he died; posthumously General of Cavalry, Equal in Honor to the Three Dukes, Governor of Qizhou, posthumous title Clear and Solemn.
idiomatic: In Xinghe year three he died; posthumously General of Cavalry, Equal in Honor to the Three Dukes, Governor of Qizhou, posthumous name Clear and Solemn.

literal: Xin Shaoxian was a man of Didao in Longxi.
idiomatic: Xin Shaoxian came from Didao in Longxi.

literal: His fifth-generation ancestor Yi was Governor of Youzhou under Jin.
idiomatic: Fifth-generation ancestor Yi was Jin's Governor of Youzhou.

literal: His father Shen served Western Liang as General of Valiant Cavalry.
idiomatic: His father Shen was General of Valiant Cavalry under Western Liang.

literal: When Liang's last ruler Xin fought Zuju Mengxun at Liaooquan the army was defeated; Xin lost his horse; Shen gave the mount he rode to Xin and himself died in the calamity.
idiomatic: When the last Liang ruler Xin fought Mengxun at Liaooquan and lost his horse, Shen gave him his mount and died in the rout.

literal: For righteous valor he was famed in the western lands.
idiomatic: His sacrifice won fame in the west.

literal: When Liangzhou was pacified Shaoxian moved inward and made his home at Jinyang.
idiomatic: When Liangzhou fell Shaoxian moved inland to Jinyang.

literal: Clever and perceptive with judgment, he was very friendly with Guangping's You Minggen, Fanyang's Lu Dushi, and his fellow commandery-man Li Chengshao.
idiomatic: Bright and discerning, he befriended You Minggen of Guangping, Lu Dushi of Fanyang, and Li Chengshao of his commandery.

literal: He had utmost nature; in mourning his father for three years his mouth knew no savor and his head knew no combing — his hair fell out entirely, so he always wore a long-skirted black cap.
idiomatic: Utterly filial, he mourned his father three years without tasting food or combing hair until it fell out; he wore a long black mourning cap thereafter.

literal: From Doctor of the Palace Secretariat he was transferred Director of the Spirit Department.
idiomatic: He rose from Doctor of the Palace Secretariat to Director of the Spirit Department.

literal: In Huangxing Xue Anyi surrendered Pengcheng to Wei.
idiomatic: In Huangxing Xue Anyi surrendered Pengcheng to Wei.

literal: The court then wished to soothe the newly attached; Shaoxian was made Governor of Xiapi.
idiomatic: The court wished to soothe new subjects and made Shaoxian Governor of Xiapi.

literal: His government was not very scrutinizing — he raised only what was out of line and otherwise taught people to build livelihood and prepare against bandits.
idiomatic: He ruled lightly, correcting only gross abuses and teaching people to prosper and guard against raiders.

literal: When Song generals Chen Xianda, Xiao Daocheng, and Xiao Shunzhi came to raid, Daocheng told Shunzhi: "Xin Shaoxian is not easy to invade — we should together be cautious.
idiomatic: When Song's Chen Xianda, Xiao Daocheng, and Xiao Shunzhi raided, Daocheng told Shunzhi, "Xin Shaoxian is not easy prey — be careful together."

literal: " Therefore they did not cross the commandery border but camped straight at Lüliang.
idiomatic: They did not enter the commandery but camped at Lüliang.

literal: He died in the commandery; posthumously Governor of Bingzhou and Marquis of Jinyang, posthumous title Kind.
idiomatic: He died in office; posthumously Governor of Bingzhou and Marquis of Jinyang, posthumous name Kind.

literal: His son Fengda loved the Way and delighted in antiquity; he had the name of an elder.
idiomatic: His son Fengda loved the Way and antiquity and was called a man of stature.

literal: He died as Regular Attendant in the state of Prince of Jingzhao Zitui.
idiomatic: He died Regular Attendant to Prince Zitui of Jingzhao.

literal: Fengda's son Xiang, styled Wanfu.
idiomatic: Fengda's son Xiang, styled Wanfu.

literal: Recommended as Xiuzhou provincial graduate, twice promoted to Chief Clerk of the Ministry of Works.
idiomatic: A Xiuzhou graduate, he twice rose to Chief Clerk of the Ministry of Works.

literal: The consort of Prince of Xianyang Xi was the younger sister of Xiang's wife.
idiomatic: Prince Xi of Xianyang's consort was sister to Xiang's wife.

literal: When Xi plotted rebellion, kin and friends mostly fell into slander; Xiang alone stood apart and took no part.
idiomatic: When Xi rebelled, kin and friends were ruined; Xiang alone kept clear.

literal: He was transferred Military Secretary of the Pingbei Headquarters in Bingzhou.
idiomatic: He became Military Secretary of Bingzhou's Pingbei Headquarters.

literal: A returned soldier from Baibi named Yao Daoxian was accused as a bandit; all officials suspected him.
idiomatic: A Baibi soldier, Yao Daoxian, was accused of banditry; officials doubted him.

literal: Xiang said: "Daoxian's face bears grief.
idiomatic: Xiang said, "Daoxian's face shows grief.

literal: To judge a prison case by complexion — is this not that saying?"
idiomatic: To read guilt in the face — is this not that very thing?"

literal: He firmly insisted on his behalf.
idiomatic: He pressed hard for him.

literal: After more than a month the real bandits were captured elsewhere.
idiomatic: A month later the real bandits were caught elsewhere.

literal: Later he was made Longma Headquarters Secretary in Yingzhou, concurrently Governor of Yiyang.
idiomatic: Later he was Longma Headquarters Secretary in Yingzhou, concurrently Governor of Yiyang.

literal: When Bai Zaosheng rebelled Liang sent aid; because of this garrisons along the Huai surrendered in succession.
idiomatic: When Bai Zaosheng rebelled Liang sent help; Huai garrisons fell one after another.

literal: Only Xiang held the city firm.
idiomatic: Only Xiang held firm.

literal: Liang also sent generals Hu Wucheng and Tao Pinglu; on Golden Mountain south of the province they linked camps and pressed.
idiomatic: Liang sent Hu Wucheng and Tao Pinglu to camp on Golden Mountain south of the province and press the siege.

literal: Xiang struck where they did not expect.
idiomatic: Xiang struck unexpectedly.

literal: The bandits collapsed greatly; he captured Pinglu, beheaded Wucheng, and sent them to the capital.
idiomatic: The enemy broke; he seized Pinglu, beheaded Wucheng, and sent heads to court.

literal: The province was wholly preserved.
idiomatic: The province was saved entire.

literal: Merit was about to be rewarded when Governor Lou Yue, shamed that the achievement ranked below his, spoke against it to the administration — in the end it was not carried out.
idiomatic: Rewards were due when Governor Lou Yue, ashamed the glory outshone him, slandered him at court — nothing came of it.

literal: When Hu bandit Liu Longju rebelled in Huazhou, Xiang was made Military Secretary of Prince of Anding Xie's Pacification Headquarters and also Separate Commander; with the Hu-pacification envoy Xue He he destroyed them.
idiomatic: When Liu Longju rebelled in Huazhou, Xiang served Prince Xie of Anding as Military Secretary and Separate Commander and with Xue He destroyed the rebels.

literal: He died; posthumously Governor of Southern Qingzhou.
idiomatic: He died; posthumously Governor of Southern Qingzhou.

literal: Xiang's younger brother Shaoyong, styled Jihe, was clever in youth, filial in conduct, and especially loved by grandfather Shaoxian.
idiomatic: Younger brother Shaoyong, styled Jihe, was bright and filial and especially loved by grandfather Shaoxian.

literal: Shaoxian by nature loved sheep liver and often called Shaoyong to eat with him.
idiomatic: Shaoxian loved sheep liver and often shared it with Shaoyong.

literal: When Shaoxian died Shaoyong never ate liver all his life.
idiomatic: After Shaoxian died Shaoyong never touched liver again.

literal: By nature humane and thick, with ritual propriety — household law within the gates was weighty in the age.
idiomatic: Humane and courteous, his household rules were famed.

literal: He was gradually promoted Field Bureau Attendant under the Ministry of Works and Prince of Gaoyang Yong.
idiomatic: He rose to Field Bureau Attendant under the Ministry of Works and Prince Yong of Gaoyang.

literal: Shaoyong was upright and clear, not fearing the powerful; lawsuits piled for years — he decided them on the spot.
idiomatic: Upright and fearless, he ended lawsuits years old in a single sitting.

literal: The path of patronage was cut off; the age called him wise and bright.
idiomatic: Favor-seekers found no door; men called him wise.

literal: In Zhengshi an edict had every office recommend those it knew; Prince Yong of Gaoyang and Personnel Director Li Xian both put Shaoyong first.
idiomatic: In Zhengshi each office was to recommend talent; Prince Yong and Li Xian of Personnel both named Shaoyong first.

literal: He died as Supervisor in the Palace.
idiomatic: He died Supervisor in the Palace.

literal: Shaoyong's wife the Wang clan had virtue and righteousness.
idiomatic: His wife of the Wang clan had virtue.

literal: Shaoyong and his cousin Huairen's brothers dwelt together.
idiomatic: Shaoyong lived with cousin Huairen's household.

literal: Huairen and the others served him very respectfully; ritual courtesy within the women's quarters — no one found fault.
idiomatic: Huairen's family served him scrupulously; no one faulted their courtesy.

literal: Scholar-officials for this praised them.
idiomatic: Scholars praised them for it.

literal: His son Yuanhuan; in Wuding era, Military Secretary of the Equal-in-Honor Headquarters.
idiomatic: His son Yuanhuan was Military Secretary of an Equal-in-Honor Headquarters in Wuding.

literal: Yuanhuan's younger brother Xunshi was Administrative Clerk in the Grand Preceptor's Office.
idiomatic: Younger brother Xunshi was clerk in the Grand Preceptor's office.

literal: Fengda's younger brother Mu, styled Shuzong, was recommended as Maocai and became Aide of Eastern Yongzhou.
idiomatic: Fengda's younger brother Mu, styled Shuzong, was a Maocai graduate and Aide of Eastern Yongzhou.

literal: At first he followed his father in Xiapi and was friendly with Pengcheng's Chen Jingwen.
idiomatic: He first followed his father to Xiapi and befriended Chen Jingwen of Pengcheng.

literal: Jingwen's younger brother Jingwu in youth became a monk, followed teachers far to study, and long did not return.
idiomatic: Brother Jingwu became a monk and studied abroad for years without return.

literal: Jingwen, ill and near death, entrusted twenty bolts of mixed silk to Mu for Jingwu.
idiomatic: Dying, Jingwen entrusted twenty bolts of silk to Mu for Jingwu.

literal: Mu long could not see him; after twenty years he met Jingwu in Luoyang and returned the goods — the seal and inscription as before.
idiomatic: Twenty years later Mu met Jingwu in Luoyang and returned the bundle sealed as before.

literal: The age called him honest and faithful.
idiomatic: Men praised his honesty.

literal: He held in succession Military Secretary of Eastern Jingzhou, then Chief Clerk, concurrently Governor of Yiyang, commanding the garrison.
idiomatic: He was Military Secretary then Chief Clerk of Eastern Jingzhou, concurrently Governor of Yiyang, commanding the garrison.

literal: He elegantly had a will to pity people.
idiomatic: He was known for compassion.

literal: Again transferred Governor of Ruyang.
idiomatic: He became Governor of Ruyang.

literal: Meeting flood and famine he memorialized asking to lighten land tax.
idiomatic: Floods brought famine; he asked to lighten taxes.

literal: The emperor approved it and then ordered the whole commandery of Ruyang permitted to pay tribute in small silk.
idiomatic: The emperor agreed and let all Ruyang pay tribute in light silk.

literal: He was made Administrator of Pingyuan.
idiomatic: He was made Administrator of Pingyuan.

literal: Summoned as General Who Pacifies the Barbarians and Grand Master of Palace Counsel — before he set out he died in the commandery.
idiomatic: Summoned as General Who Pacifies the Barbarians and Grand Master of Palace Counsel, he died in office before departing.

literal: Posthumously Rear General and Governor of Youzhou.
idiomatic: Posthumously Rear General and Governor of Youzhou.

literal: His son Zifu, styled Yuanying, early had learning and conduct, and rose through posts to Administrator of Pingyuan.
idiomatic: His son Zifu, styled Yuanying, was learned early and rose to Administrator of Pingyuan.

literal: Father and son both held this commandery; officials and people cherished and were at ease with them.
idiomatic: Father and son both governed Pingyuan; the people loved them.

literal: When Yuan Hao entered Luoyang Zifu did not follow.
idiomatic: When Yuan Hao took Luoyang Zifu would not follow.

literal: When Emperor Zhuang restored the government he was enfeoffed Baron of Sanmen.
idiomatic: When Emperor Zhuang returned to power he was made Baron of Sanmen.

literal: In Tianping he was made Military Secretary of the Grand Preceptor's Office.
idiomatic: In Tianping he was Military Secretary of the Grand Preceptor's Office.

literal: White Mountain linked the three Qi; on the borders of several prefectures around Xiaqiu there were many bandits.
idiomatic: White Mountain linked the three Qi; around Xiaqiu bandits were many.

literal: Zifu received orders to inspect; he thereby distinguished valleys and passes where garrisons should stand.
idiomatic: Ordered to inspect, he mapped passes where garrisons should stand.

literal: Also the powerful families of the provinces.
idiomatic: Provincial magnates as well

literal: cast metal in the mountains; many villainous factions relied on them and could also secretly forge weapons.
idiomatic: smelted in the hills; outlaws clustered there and secretly forged weapons.

literal: He memorialized asking to break up and abolish all smelting works.
idiomatic: He asked to shut every illicit foundry.

literal: The court approved and followed it.
idiomatic: The court approved.
